question_text:
Two thin wires, Wire-1 of diameter $0.650$ mm and Wire-2 of unknown diameter $d$ are given. To obtain the value of $d$, the diameters of the two wires are measured with a screw gauge. The screw gauge has a pitch of $0.5$ mm and there are $100$ divisions on the circular scale (CS). The smallest division on the linear scale (LS) is $0.5$ mm. The table shows the readings of LS and CS for the measurements. The value of $d$ (in $\mu$m) is:
Readings
LS (mm)CS
Wire-1$0.5$$42$
Wire-2$1.5$$95$
solution_text:
The least count (LC) of the screw gauge is given by:

$\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of divisions on CS}} = \dfrac{0.5}{100} = 0.005 \text{ mm}$

For Wire-1, the measured reading is:

$\text{Reading}_1 = \text{LS} + \text{CS} \times \text{LC}$

$\text{Reading}_1 = 0.5 + 42 \times 0.005 = 0.5 + 0.210 = 0.710 \text{ mm}$

The actual diameter of Wire-1 is $0.650 \text{ mm}$. The zero error of the screw gauge is:

$\text{Zero Error} = \text{Measured Reading} - \text{Actual Value} = 0.710 - 0.650 = +0.060 \text{ mm}$

For Wire-2, the measured reading is:

$\text{Reading}_2 = \text{LS} + \text{CS} \times \text{LC}$

$\text{Reading}_2 = 1.5 + 95 \times 0.005 = 1.5 + 0.475 = 1.975 \text{ mm}$

The actual diameter $d$ of Wire-2 is obtained by subtracting the zero error from its measured reading:

$d = \text{Reading}_2 - \text{Zero Error} = 1.975 - 0.060 = 1.915 \text{ mm}$

Converting the diameter into micrometers ($\mu$m):

$d = 1.915 \times 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m} = 1915 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$

Answer: $1915$

question_text: There are two vernier calipers both of which have 1 cm divided into 10 equal divisions on the main scale. The Vernier scale of one of the calipers C1 has 10 equal divisions that correspond to 9 main scale divisions. The Vernier scale of the other caliper C2 has 10 equal divisions that correspond to 11 main scale divisions. The readings of the two calipers are shown in the figure. The measured values (in cm) by calipers C1 and C2 respectively, are
solution_text:
For caliper C1

10 VSD=9 MSD

LC=1 MSD-1 VSD

LC=0.01 cm

Measured value=Main scale reading+vernier scale reading×least count

=2.8+7×0.01 cm

=2.87 cm

For caliper C2

10 VSD=11 MSD

LC=-0.01 cm (Negative least count means we have to take VSR from the right of the scale 10‐7)

Measured value =2.8+10-7×0.01 cm

=2.83 cm

question_text: During an experiment with a metre bridge, the galvanometer shows a null point when the jockey is pressed at 40.0 cm using a standard resistance of 90 Ω ,as shown in the figure. The least count of the scale used in the metre bridge is 1mm. The unknown resistance is
solution_text:
The unknown resistance is given by, R=x100-x90
Putting x=40.0 cm, R=60 Ω

For error analysis, R=40.0±0.1100.0-40.0±0.1×90=40.0±0.160.0±0.1×90
In multiplication and division, fractional errors get added up.

Therefore, ∆RR=0.140+0.160
⇒∆R=1004060×0.1×60=0.25 Ω
Hence, R=60±0.25 Ω

question_text: A vernier calipers has $1 \mathrm{~mm}$ marks on the main scale. It has 20 equal divisions on the vernier scale which match with 16 main scale divisions. For this vernier calipers, the least count is
solution_text:
Least count of vernier calipers
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { LC }=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \text { VSD } \\
& =\frac{\text { Smallest division on main scale }}{\text { Number of divisions on vernier scale }} \\
& 20 \text { divisions of vernier scale } \\
& =16 \text { divisions of main scale } \\
& \therefore \quad 1 \mathrm{VSD}=\frac{16}{20} \mathrm{~mm}=0.8 \mathrm{~mm} \\
& \therefore \quad \text { LC }=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{VSD} \\
& =1 \mathrm{~mm}-0.8 \mathrm{~mm} \\
& \therefore \quad=0.2 \mathrm{~mm} \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$
$\therefore$ The correct option is (d).

The circular scale of a screw gauge has 50 divisions and pitch of $0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$. Find the diameter of sphere. Main scale reading is 2 .
solution_text:
Least count $\mathrm{LC}=\frac{\text { Pitch }}{\text { Number of divisions on circular scale }}=\frac{0.1}{50}$ $=0.01 \mathrm{~mm}$
Now, diameter of ball $=(2 \times 0.5 \mathrm{~mm})+(25-5)(0.01)=1.2 \mathrm{~mm}$
